units.title: Seminar 7 · Time series: moving averages and the seasonal component

bites.title: Moving averages: smoothing a time series
bites.html:
A moving average replaces each value by the mean of a short “window” around it. Moving the window along the series gives a smoothed series, which is the trend component trt.

  • Odd length m = 2p + 1: a simple mean of p values before t, yt and p values after t.
  • The first p and the last p time points get no moving average.
  • The higher m, the smoother the result.

bites.title: Which length m?
bites.html:
From the lecture: if the series has a seasonal component, choose m equal to the length of seasonality s.

  • Quarterly data → m = 4
  • Daily data with a weekly pattern → m = 7
  • Monthly data → m = 12

If m is even (4, 12), use the centred moving average: the mean of two neighbouring windows, so it lands exactly on a time point t.

Moving averages cannot predict the future: the ends of the series are missing.

bites.title: First moving average of a daily series (exercise ts_mov7)
bites.intro: Week 1: Mo 6, Tu 7, We 8, Th 9, Fr 8, Sa 2, Su 1. Daily data with a weekly pattern.

steps.html: Seasonality is weekly, so m = s = 7 (odd), m = 2p + 1 gives p = 3.
The first moving average is centred on t = p + 1 = 4, the Thursday of week 1.
Next one: drop Monday of week 1, add Monday of week 2 (8): ȳ<sub>5</sub> = (7 + 8 + 9 + 8 + 2 + 1 + 8) / 7 = 6.1429.

bites.q: Monthly data with a seasonal pattern. Which moving average?
bites.why: m = length of seasonality = 12 months, and 12 is even, so centred.

bites.title: Seasonal component: differences or indices
bites.html:
The seasonal component st shows how much a season (quarter, month, day) pushes the values up or down.

  • Additive decomposition yt = trt + st + et, when seasonal variations are stable in time → seasonal differences sdj, in the same units as the series. They add up to 0.
  • Multiplicative decomposition yt = trt · st · et, when seasonal variations are not stable → seasonal indices sij, relative (no units). They add up to s.

sd1 = −18.06 means season 1 is on average 18.06 units below the trend. si1 = 0.693 means about 30.7 % below the trend.

bites.title: Simple approach: four steps
bites.html:
1. Trend trt by moving averages with m = s.
  2. For each t that has trt: yt − trt (additive) or yt / trt (multiplicative).
  3. Mean of these values for each season j: the mean seasonal difference or mean seasonal index.
  4. Adjust them: differences so they add up to 0, indices so they add up to s.

bites.title: Simple approach to the seasonal component

bites.q: A seasonal index si = 1.20 for December means…
options: December values are on average about 20 % above the trend
December is 1.20 units above the trend
bites.why: Seasonal indices are relative: 1.20 = 120 % of the trend value.

bites.title: Regression approach (quarterly, linear trend)
bites.html:
Trend and seasonality are estimated together with a regression with dummy variables x1, x2, x3 (xj = 1 in quarter j, otherwise 0):

ŷt = b0* + b1t + a1x1 + a2x2 + a3x3 (parameters from Excel)

  1. ā = (a1 + a2 + a3) / 4
  2. b0 = b0* + ā, so the trend is trt = b0 + b1t
  3. sdj = aj − ā for j = 1, 2, 3, and sd4 = −ā
  4. Prediction: ŷt = b0 + b1t + sdj

bites.title: Visitors of a cultural centre (exercise ts_seas5)
bites.intro: ŷt = 34.75 + 2.53125 t − 12.40625 x1 − 21.9375 x2 − 13.46875 x3 (thousands of visitors, quarterly, 2012Q1–2014Q4)

bites.title: Events and their probability
bites.html:
A random experiment is something whose outcome you cannot predict for sure, like rolling a die. An event (A, B, …) is a group of outcomes, for example “an even number falls”.

  • Certain event: P(E) = 1
  • Impossible event: P(Ø) = 0
  • Random event: 0 < P(A) < 1

Classical probability: P(A) = m / n, favourable outcomes divided by all equally likely outcomes. One six on a fair die: 1/6.

bites.title: Combining events
bites.html:
• Intersection A ∩ B: both happen.
  • Union A ∪ B: at least one happens.
  • Disjoint (mutually exclusive): they cannot happen together, P(A ∩ B) = 0.
  • Complementary Ā: “A does not happen”, P(Ā) = 1 − P(A).
  • Independent: one does not change the probability of the other, P(A|B) = P(A). Then P(A ∩ B) = P(A)·P(B).

Tip from the lecture: “at least one” is usually easiest as 1 − P(none).

bites.title: Probability rules
bites.html: Independent events → multiply. Dependent events (e.g. drawing without replacement) → multiply by the conditional probability.

bites.title: Two alarm systems (lecture example)
bites.intro: A bank has two independent alarm systems, 90 % and 80 % efficient. What is the probability that at least one detects a burglary?

steps.html: Name the events: A = 1st system detects, P(A) = 0.9; B = 2nd system detects, P(B) = 0.8.
“At least one” = the union A ∪ B. Use the addition rule: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B).
The systems are independent, so P(A ∩ B) = P(A)·P(B) = 0.9 · 0.8 = 0.72.
Answer in words: the probability that at least one system detects a burglary is 98 %.

bites.q: Two events cannot happen at the same time. What are they called?
bites.why: Disjoint events have an empty intersection, P(A ∩ B) = 0. Independent events can happen together; they just don’t influence each other.

bites.q: You need P(at least one success). What is usually the quickest way?
bites.why: “At least one” is the complement of “none”, so P = 1 − P(none).

bites.title: Random variables
bites.html:
A random variable X gets its value from a random experiment (e.g. the number of siblings of a randomly chosen person).

  • Discrete: countable values (0, 1, 2, …). Described by the probability function P(x) = P(X = x), and all P(x) add up to 1.
  • Continuous: any value in an interval. Described by the density f(x). P(X = one exact value) = 0.

Both have the distribution function F(x) = P(X ≤ x): the probability of “x or less”.

bites.title: Expected value, variance, quantiles
bites.html:
• Expected value E(X) = Σ x·P(x): the long-run average, like a weighted mean.
  • Variance Var(X) = Σ x²·P(x) − [E(X)]²: how spread out the values are.
  • Standard deviation S.D.(X) = √Var(X).
  • 100·P % quantile xP: F(xP) = P. 100·P % of the values are lower, the rest higher.

bites.title: Random variable formulas
bites.html: For a table of x and P(x): add the right P(x) values for probabilities, multiply x·P(x) for the expected value.

steps.html: In words: a randomly chosen person has 0.98 siblings on average.

bites.q: What does F(3) mean for a discrete random variable?
options: P(X ≤ 3), the probability of 3 or less
bites.why: The distribution function adds up all probabilities up to and including x.

bites.title: With or without replacement?
bites.html:
This one question decides the distribution:

  • With replacement: an element can be picked again, so the probability stays the same in every trial (independent trials) → binomial.
  • Without replacement: each element at most once, so the probabilities change (dependent trials) → hypergeometric.

The seminar file says: before any calculation, write down the event A, the random variable X and its distribution with parameters. Finish with a sentence in words.

bites.title: Binomial distribution, X ~ Bi(n, π)
bites.html:
• The same trial is repeated n times, independently.
  • Each trial is a success (probability π) or a failure (1 − π).
  • X = number of successes, x = 0, 1, …, n.

The combination number “n choose x” is nCr on a calculator. E(X) = nπ.

bites.title: One ace in three draws, with replacement (lecture example)
bites.intro: Three cards are drawn with replacement from 32 cards with 4 aces. Probability of exactly one ace?

steps.html: Event A: an ace is drawn in one trial, π = 4/32 = 0.125.
X = number of aces in 3 independent trials, so X ~ Bi(3, 0.125).
In words: the probability that exactly one of the three cards is an ace is about 28.7 %.

bites.title: Hypergeometric distribution, X ~ Hy(N, M, n)
bites.html:
• N = population size
  • M = number of “successes” in the population
  • n = sample size, drawn without replacement

Same three cards as before but without replacement: P(1) = (4 choose 1)(28 choose 2) / (32 choose 3) ≈ 30.5 %.

If n < 0.05·N you may approximate it by Bi(n, M/N).

bites.q: 5 cards are dealt from a deck (no card returned). Which distribution counts the aces?
bites.why: Without replacement the trials are dependent, so the hypergeometric distribution.

bites.title: Poisson distribution, X ~ Po(λ)
bites.html:
Use it for the number of occurrences in an interval of time, length, area… (calls per hour, misprints per page).

  • λ = average number of occurrences in your interval. Rescale it first with a simple proportion: 15 buses per hour → λ = 1 bus per 4 minutes.
  • E(X) = Var(X) = λ.

bites.title: No bus in 4 minutes (lecture example)
bites.intro: On average 15 buses arrive per hour. Probability that no bus arrives within 4 minutes?

steps.html: Rescale λ: 15 per 60 minutes → 15 · 4/60 = 1 bus per 4 minutes, so X ~ Po(1).
In words: the probability that no bus arrives within 4 minutes is about 36.8 %.

bites.title: Approximations
bites.html:
• Hypergeometric → binomial if n < 0.05·N, with π = M/N.
  • Binomial → Poisson if π ≤ 0.1 and n > 30, with λ = n·π.

Lecture example: Bi(40, 0.05) gives P(2) = 0.2777, Po(2) gives 0.2707. Close enough.

bites.title: Normal distribution, X ~ N(μ, σ²)
bites.html:
The most important continuous distribution, bell-shaped and symmetric around μ.

  1. Standardize: z = (x − μ) / σ.
  2. Look up Φ(z) in Table I. For negative z use Φ(−z) = 1 − Φ(z).
  3. “Higher than”: 1 − Φ(z). “Between”: Φ(z₂) − Φ(z₁).

Quantiles: xP = μ + σ·zP, with zP from Table II. Careful: the problem gives the variance σ² or the standard deviation σ, so read which one.

bites.why: The second parameter is the variance σ² = 25, so σ = 5.

bites.title: t, chi-square and F: reading the tables
bites.html:
• t-distribution t(df): symmetric around 0, so tP = −t1−P (low quantiles are negative). Table III. For large df it is close to the normal.
  • Chi-square χ²(df): only values ≥ 0. Table IV.
  • F-distribution F(df₁, df₂): only values ≥ 0. Table V (95 % quantiles). The order of df₁ and df₂ matters.

These are the tables you will use in every hypothesis test in Seminars 11 and 12.

bites.why: The t-distribution is symmetric around zero: t0.05 = −t0.95.

bites.title: Population and sample
bites.html:
Inferential statistics draws conclusions about a whole population (size N) from a random sample (size n).

  • A population parameter (e.g. E(X), π) is one fixed but unknown number.
  • A sample statistic (e.g. the sample mean) changes from sample to sample: it is a random variable.

The lecture warns: justified inference needs a random sample from a clearly defined population. An internet questionnaire usually is not one.

bites.title: Point estimate
bites.html:
A point estimate is one number: the value of the sample statistic.

  • Population mean → sample mean x̄
  • Population proportion → p = nj / n
  • Count in the population → N·p

Before calculating, name the population, the variable and the parameter of interest (from the seminar file).

bites.title: Confidence interval
bites.html:
A confidence interval is a range built around the point estimate that is likely to cover the unknown parameter. The confidence level 1 − α (e.g. 95 %) is roughly the share of such intervals that would cover the parameter if we took many samples.

Which formula?

  • Normal distribution in the population and σ² unknown → t with n − 1 degrees of freedom.
  • “Random sample size assumed to be large enough” → z.

For a 95 % interval α = 0.05, so you need the quantile 1 − α/2 = 0.975.

bites.title: Size of items (lecture example)
bites.intro: 400 items: x̄ = 116 mm, s = 4.081 mm. Construct a 92 % two-sided confidence interval for the mean size (large sample).

steps.html: Large sample → z. 1 − α = 0.92, so α = 0.08 and you need z<sub>1−α/2</sub> = z<sub>0.96</sub> = 1.751 (Table II).
In words: a two-sided 92 % confidence interval for the mean size of all items in the delivery, based on this random sample of 400 items, is (115.64; 116.36) mm.

bites.q: Normal distribution, n = 20, σ² unknown. Which quantile do you need for a 95 % interval?
bites.why: Normal population with unknown variance → t with n − 1 = 19 df, at 1 − α/2 = 0.975.

bites.title: Width of the interval
bites.html:
Assuming nothing else changes:

  • Higher confidence level → wider interval → less accurate.
  • Bigger sample → narrower interval → more accurate.

Half the width is the maximum acceptable (sampling) error Δ.

bites.q: You raise the confidence level from 90 % to 99 % and keep the same sample. What happens to the interval?
bites.why: A higher confidence level needs a bigger quantile, so the interval is wider.

bites.title: Proportion and count
bites.html:
For a proportion (large sample): p ± z1−α/2·√(p(1 − p)/n), with p = nj/n.

For a count in the population (N known): multiply both limits by N.

Judging a hypothesis: if the claimed value lies inside the interval, the results are not inconsistent with it.

bites.title: Expired cans (lecture example)
bites.intro: 59 of 320 randomly chosen cans had expired. 99.8 % confidence interval for the proportion of expired cans?

steps.html: A research hypothesis “15 % of cans have expired” is not inconsistent with this result, because 0.15 lies inside the interval.

units.title: Seminar 11 · Hypothesis tests: mean, proportion, goodness of fit

bites.title: What a hypothesis test does
bites.html:
You have a claim about a population (e.g. “the mean birth weight is 3,500 g”) and a random sample. The test decides whether the sample is consistent with the claim.

  • H0 (null hypothesis): the parameter equals the claimed value.
  • H1 (alternative): what you want to show, >, < or ≠.
  • Significance level α (e.g. 5 %): how much risk of wrongly rejecting H0 you accept.

bites.title: The five steps (always the same)
bites.html:
1. State H0 and H1.
  2. Recognise the test statistic and its distribution.
  3. Calculate the value of the test statistic.
  4. Form the rejection region Wα with quantiles from the tables.
  5. Give a conclusion in words.

Conclusion wording from the seminar file:

  • Value in W: “the value of the test statistic is inconsistent with H0 in favour of H1 that …”
  • Value not in W: “the value of the test statistic is not inconsistent with H0 that …”

bites.title: Which tail? H1 decides
bites.html:
• H1 with > → right tail: W = {z ≥ z1−α}
  • H1 with < → left tail: W = {z ≤ −z1−α}
  • H1 with ≠ → both tails: W = {|z| ≥ z1−α/2}

Read the story: “worried about a decline” → <. “Doesn’t want it higher” → >. “Is it the same / is there a difference” → ≠.

bites.title: Tests of the mean and proportion
bites.html: Same choice as with intervals: normal population with σ² unknown → t; large sample → z; proportion → z with π₀ in the denominator.

bites.title: Birth weight (worked in the seminar file)
bites.intro: Healthy populations: mean 3,500 g. Affected region: 50 babies, x̄ = 3,310 g, s = 500 g. α = 1 %. Is the mean lower?

steps.html: H0: E(X) = 3,500 g. H1: E(X) < 3,500 g (the activists claim it is lower).
Large sample, general distribution → Z = (X̄ − μ₀)/S · √n, approximately N(0, 1) if H0 is true.

−2.687 ≤ −2.326, so z is in W. At a 1 % significance level, the value of the test statistic is inconsistent with H0 in favour of H1 that the mean birth weight in the affected region is lower than in healthy populations.

bites.q: H1: E(X) ≠ 28,306 and α = 0.06. Which quantile is the critical value?
In a test of a proportion, what goes under the square root?
options: π₀(1 − π₀)/n, the value from H0
bites.why: In the test we assume H0 is true, so we use π₀. (In a confidence interval we use p.)

bites.title: Chi-square goodness-of-fit test
bites.html:
Tests whether the whole distribution matches an assumption (e.g. 52 % supermarket, 18 % shopping centre, …).

  1. H0: πj = π0,j for all categories. H1: non H0.
  2. Expected frequencies: n′j = n·π0,j.
  3. g = Σ (nj − n′j)² / n′j
  4. W = {g ≥ χ²1−α(k − 1)}, where k is the number of categories. Always the right tail.

bites.q: A goodness-of-fit test has 6 categories. How many degrees of freedom?
